name: Licensing Synthetic Assets and Likeness
title: Licensing Synthetic Assets and Likeness
answer: This page covers the licensing of AI-generated or AI-modified assets, including synthetic images, audio, video, text, and digital representations of a person's face, voice, or persona. It addresses how rights in these assets are identified, cleared, and transferred across advertising, entertainment, gaming, and product design. The focus is on the overlap of copyright, trademark, right of publicity, and contract terms that determine who may use a synthetic asset, for what purpose, and for how long. It also covers licensing of underlying models or datasets only where those terms flow through to the output asset.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers the licensing of AI-generated or AI-modified assets, including synthetic images, audio, video, text, and digital representations of a person's face, voice, or persona. It addresses how rights in these assets are identified, cleared, and transferred across advertising, entertainment, gaming, and product design. The focus is on the overlap of copyright, trademark, right of publicity, and contract terms that determine who may use a synthetic asset, for what purpose, and for how long. It also covers licensing of underlying models or datasets only where those terms flow through to the output asset.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Licensing synthetic assets runs on standard IP licensing infrastructure: contract templates, rights clearance databases, digital asset management systems, and metadata standards for provenance. For likeness, it relies on consent records, talent agreements, and guild or union terms where applicable. Some workflows attach license terms directly to a file through embedded provenance metadata, but adoption remains uneven. The practical infrastructure is therefore a mix of legal documents, asset registries, and lightweight technical markers rather than a single platform.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins by identifying what rights exist in a synthetic asset, which often means separating human-authored elements from model-generated output, since copyright protection for purely generated material is uncertain. For a likeness, the practitioner obtains a written consent or release from the person depicted, covering the specific use, term, territory, and any alterations. The license then combines the appropriate grants: a copyright or content license for the asset, a trademark license for any brand elements, and a publicity release for any recognizable person. Due diligence includes reviewing the generative model's terms of service and the provenance of training data, because restrictions upstream can limit what a downstream license may grant.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights in synthetic assets are often layered: copyright in the generated expression, trademark in any brand elements, and a personal right in a recognizable likeness or voice. Risk concentrates where a synthetic asset is indistinguishable from a real person or brand, because consent, endorsement, and passing-off claims can arise even without copying protected expression. Provenance systems that record the model, prompt, training data, and consent chain reduce this risk, but many licenses still rely on contractual warranties rather than technical verification. The site's tracker of 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, reflects how contested these questions have become.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Licensing is moving toward standardized clauses for AI training, output ownership, and likeness consent, driven by model providers and large content buyers. Expect more machine-readable license terms attached to assets through provenance metadata, so downstream users can verify permissions automatically. As state right-of-publicity and deepfake laws multiply, including many of the 6,823 state AI bills tracked on this site, licenses will need to account for jurisdiction-specific consent and labeling duties. Case law on whether AI-generated works are copyrightable will also determine how much value a synthetic asset license can actually transfer.
